title: Isogeny-based Cryptography Wiki
text: Welcome to the Isogeny-based Cryptography Wiki. This site serves as an open-source, mathematically rigorous, and accessible repository of knowledge detailing post-quantum cryptographic protocols built on the hardness of finding isogenies between elliptic curves.

title: FESTA
text:
FESTA is a public-key encryption (PKE) protocol that creatively repurposes the devastating attacks on the Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman (SIDH) protocol. While SIDH’s security was compromised by torsion-point attacks when auxiliary torsion information is revealed, FESTA relies on a novel trapdoor function where these very attacks are leveraged by the legitimate trapdoor holder to invert a one-way function.
By scaling the revealed torsion points with a secret matrix, FESTA prevents malicious attackers from utilizing the SIDH attacks [BaMaPo23]. Using standard transformations (like OAEP), this trapdoor mechanism enables the construction of an efficient IND-CCA secure PKE in the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM).

title: FESTA
text:
2 Protocol Design
The foundation of FESTA is an injective trapdoor function evaluated over supersingular elliptic curves.
E0EAE1E2µPbQb¶µRASA¶=Aµ'A(Pb)'A(Qb)¶Bµ'1(Pb)'1(Qb)¶Bµ'2(RA)'2(SA)¶'A'1'2Ã

2.1 Global Parameters

\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) (chosen with \(j(E_0) \neq 0, 1728\) to avoid non-trivial automorphisms).
\(\langle P_b, Q_b \rangle = E_0[2^b]\): A canonical basis for the \(2^b\)-torsion on \(E_0\).
\(\mathcal{M}_b\): A set of commutative, invertible diagonal matrices over \((\mathbb{Z}/2^b\mathbb{Z})^\times\) modulo \(\langle -I_2 \rangle\).



2.2 Setup and Key Generation
The trapdoor key generation works as follows:

Compute a secret \(d_A\)-isogeny \(\varphi_A: E_0 \rightarrow E_A\).
Sample a random matrix \(A \in \mathcal{M}_b\).
Calculate the scaled torsion images on \(E_A\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_A \\ S_A \end{pmatrix} = A \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_A(P_b) \\ \varphi_A(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]


Secret Key (Trapdoor): \((A, \varphi_A)\).
Public Key: \((E_A, R_A, S_A)\).



2.3 Function Evaluation (Forward Direction)
To evaluate the one-way function on an input consisting of two isogenies \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) (degree \(d_1\)), \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\) (degree \(d_2\)), and a matrix \(B \in \mathcal{M}_b\):

Compute \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) and \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\).
Scale the torsion basis images under \(\varphi_1\) by \(B\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_1 \\ S_1 \end{pmatrix} = B \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_1(P_b) \\ \varphi_1(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]
Scale the public torsion parameters under \(\varphi_2\) by \(B\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} = B \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_2(R_A) \\ \varphi_2(S_A) \end{pmatrix} \]


Output: The tuple \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2, S_2)\).

Without the knowledge of \(A\), the scaling by \(B\) (and natively \(A\)) thoroughly obfuscates the torsion point information, blocking the SIDH attack machinery.


2.4 Trapdoor Inversion
The trapdoor owner can invert the function by utilizing the commutativity of matrices \(A\) and \(B\):

Undo the secret scaling on \(E_2\) by applying \(d_1 A^{-1}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2' \\ S_2' \end{pmatrix} = d_1 A^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} \] Because \(A\) and \(B\) commute, this effectively isolates the scaling to just \(B\), bridging the torsion mappings between \(E_1\) and \(E_2\).
The resulting points reflect the exact unscaled images of \(R_1, S_1\) under the bridging isogeny \(\psi := \varphi_2 \circ \varphi_A \circ \hat{\varphi}_1\).
Invoke an arbitrary torsion-point attack (e.g., Kani’s criterion generalizing to higher dimensions via (2,2)-isogenies) on \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2', S_2')\) to efficiently compute \(\psi\).
Reconstruct the original kernels of \(\varphi_1, \varphi_2\) and the matrix \(B\) from \(\psi\).

title: FESTA
text:
3 Security Assumptions
FESTA introduces generalized hardness assumptions for the scaled-torsion setting:

Decisional Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (DIST): Distinguishing a curve and its scaled torsion images (via matrix \(A\)) from a random supersingular curve and random basis points.
Computational Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (CIST): Extracting the isogeny \(\varphi\) given \(E_0, E_1\), the domain basis, and the scaled target basis \(A(\varphi(P_0), \varphi(Q_0))^T\).
Computational Isogeny with Double Scaled-Torsion (CIST 2): Recovering two distinct isogenies \(\varphi, \varphi'\) given two instances of scaled target bases that use the same scaling matrix \(A\). Theorem 9 proves FESTA’s one-wayness reduces to the DIST and CIST 2 assumptions.

title: CSI-FiSh
text:
CSI-FiSh (Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Signatures with Fiat-Shamir) is an efficient isogeny-based digital signature scheme introduced by Beullens, Kleinjung, and Vercauteren [BeKlVe19].
The primary hurdle in building efficient signatures from the CSIDH group action is that evaluating the group action can be slow, and the structure of the class group \(\text{Cl}(R)\) is generally unknown. CSI-FiSh circumvents this by working with a specific parameter set where the class group can be fully computed.
CSI-FiSh relies on the same hardness assumptions outlined in the CSIDH.

title: CSI-FiSh
text:
CSI-FiSh (Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Signatures with Fiat-Shamir) is an efficient isogeny-based digital signature scheme introduced by Beullens, Kleinjung, and Vercauteren [BeKlVe19].
The primary hurdle in building efficient signatures from the CSIDH group action is that evaluating the group action can be slow, and the structure of the class group \(\text{Cl}(R)\) is generally unknown. CSI-FiSh circumvents this by working with a specific parameter set where the class group can be fully computed.
CSI-FiSh relies on the same hardness assumptions outlined in the CSIDH.

title: CSI-FiSh
text:
2 Key Mechanism
By computing the exact structure of \(\text{Cl}(R)\) for a 512-bit prime \(p\), CSI-FiSh can perform fast, uniform sampling of elements. This allows a direct, efficient adaptation of the classical Fiat-Shamir transform to the isogeny setting.

Underlying Hard Problem: The security relies on the hardness of finding paths between supersingular elliptic curves (the Vectorization Problem), similar to the security assumptions laid out in the foundational CSIDH protocol.

title: SIDH
text:
2 Protocol Design
E0EAEBEABEBAkker(ÁA)=h[mA]PA+[nA]QAiÁA(PB);ÁA(QB)ÁB(PA);ÁB(QA)ker(ÁB)=h[mB]PB+[nB]QBiker(Á0B)=h[mB]ÁA(PB)+[nB]ÁA(QB)iker(Á0A)=h[mA]ÁB(PA)+[nA]ÁB(QA)i

2.1 Public Parameters
Let \(p\) be a prime of the form \(p = \ell_A^{e_A} \ell_B^{e_B} \cdot f \pm 1\), where \(\ell_A, \ell_B\) are small distinct primes (typically \(\ell_A = 2, \ell_B = 3\)), \(e_A, e_B\) are large exponents, and \(f\) is a small cofactor making \(p\) prime.

Base Curve: A supersingular elliptic curve \(E_0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\).
Alice’s Torsion Basis: A basis \(\{P_A, Q_A\}\) for the torsion subgroup \(E_0[\ell_A^{e_A}]\).
Bob’s Torsion Basis: A basis \(\{P_B, Q_B\}\) for the torsion subgroup \(E_0[\ell_B^{e_B}]\).



2.2 Key Exchange Execution

Alice’s Key Generation:

Chooses a secret integer \(m_A \in \mathbb{Z} / \ell_A^{e_A}\mathbb{Z}\).
Defines her secret kernel generator \(R_A = P_A + [m_A]Q_A\).
Computes the secret isogeny \(\phi_A: E_0 \to E_A \cong E_0 / \langle R_A \rangle\).
Her Public Key is \((E_A, \phi_A(P_B), \phi_A(Q_B))\).

Bob’s Key Generation:

Chooses a secret integer \(m_B \in \mathbb{Z} / \ell_B^{e_B}\mathbb{Z}\).
Defines his secret kernel generator \(R_B = P_B + [m_B]Q_B\).
Computes the secret isogeny \(\phi_B: E_0 \to E_B \cong E_0 / \langle R_B \rangle\).
His Public Key is \((E_B, \phi_B(P_A), \phi_B(Q_A))\).

Shared Secret Computation:

Alice receives \((E_B, \phi_B(P_A), \phi_B(Q_A))\) and evaluates her secret linear combination on the received points to reconstruct the kernel on \(E_B\): \[S_A = \phi_B(P_A) + [m_A]\phi_B(Q_A) = \phi_B(P_A + [m_A]Q_A) = \phi_B(R_A)\]
She computes the secondary isogeny \(\phi_A': E_B \to E_{BA} \cong E_B / \langle \phi_B(R_A) \rangle\).
Bob receives \((E_A, \phi_A(P_B), \phi_A(Q_B))\) and analogously evaluates: \[S_B = \phi_A(P_B) + [m_B]\phi_A(Q_B) = \phi_A(P_B + [m_B]Q_B) = \phi_A(R_B)\]
He computes the secondary isogeny \(\phi_B': E_A \to E_{AB} \cong E_A / \langle \phi_A(R_B) \rangle\).


By the isomorphism theorems for curves, the codomain curves are isomorphic: \[E_{AB} \cong E_0 / \langle R_A, R_B \rangle \cong E_{BA}\] The shared secret key is the \(j\)-invariant \(j(E_{AB}) = j(E_{BA})\).

title: CSIDH
text:
CSIDH (Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman) is a post-quantum key exchange protocol proposed by Castryck et al. [CLMP18]. It serves as an isogeny-based analogue to traditional Diffie-Hellman key exchange, built on the framework of Couveignes, Rostovtsev, and Stolbunov (CRS).
Because CSIDH provides a truly commutative group action, it is highly versatile and serves as the mathematical foundation for more advanced primitives, such as the isogeny-based signature scheme CSI-FiSh.
Unlike SIDH (which uses non-commutative endomorphism rings), CSIDH leverages a commutative group action by restricting to supersingular elliptic curves defined over a prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) whose endomorphism rings are isomorphic to an order in an imaginary quadratic field.

title: CSIDH
text:
2 Protocol Design
Let \(p\) be a prime of the form \(p = 4 \cdot \ell_1 \cdot \ell_2 \cdots \ell_n - 1\), where \(\ell_i\) are small, distinct odd primes.

2.1 The Curve Space
We consider the set \(\mathcal{S}_R\) of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves \(E/\mathbb{F}_p\) whose \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-endomorphism ring \(\text{End}_{\mathbb{F}_p}(E)\) is exactly the order \(R = \mathbb{Z}[\pi]\), where \(\pi\) is the Frobenius endomorphism satisfying \(\pi^2 = -p\). These curves can be written in Montgomery form:
\[E_A: y^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x\]


2.2 The Class Group Action
The ideal class group \(\text{Cl}(R)\) acts freely and transitively on the set \(\mathcal{S}_R\). Given an ideal class \([\mathfrak{a}] \in \text{Cl}(R)\) and a curve class \([E] \in \mathcal{S}_R\), the group action is defined via the idealisogeny:
\[[\mathfrak{a}] * E = E / E[\mathfrak{a}]\]
Where \(E[\mathfrak{a}]\) is the intersection of the kernels of all endomorphisms in \(\mathfrak{a}\). Because \(\text{Cl}(R)\) is an abelian group, the action commutes:
\[[\mathfrak{a}] * ([\mathfrak{b}] * E) = ([\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}]) * E = [\mathfrak{b}] * ([\mathfrak{a}] * E)\]


2.3 Key Exchange Protocol
The commutativity of the group action allows a direct translation of the classical Diffie-Hellman matrix or exponentiation paradigm.

Computes \(E_A = [\mathfrak{a}] * E_0\)

Computes \(E_{BA} = [\mathfrak{a}] * E_B\)
